prompt: What other proteins are related to histones, and describe that relationship using SCOPe classification levels.
answer:
In SCOPe 2.08 (the stable release, released 2021-09-22), histones are classified in the Histone-fold superfamily a.22.1, which sits in the Histone-fold fold a.22 and the class a (All alpha proteins). Histone-fold superfamily membership is the broadest SCOPe relationship that SCOPe asserts as homology: the superfamily node reports homology_implied_by_level=true with homology_scope 'sf' and no warnings. So the proteins related to histones are the other members of a.22.1, read at the following family levels:

- a.22.1.1 Nucleosome core histones (sunid 47114): Histone H2A (47115), Histone H2B (47119), Histone H3 (47122), Histone H4 (47125), macro-H2A.1 histone domain (140396), plus an automated-matches node (193445). This family contains the canonical histones.
- a.22.1.2 Archaeal histone (sunid 47129): the search returned Methanothermus fervidus histone A and histone B nodes (sunids 68895, 68896) under this family, classified at species level in the a.22.1.2 lineage.
- a.22.1.3 TBP-associated factors, TAFs (sunid 47134): TAF(II)18, TAF(II)20 (histone fold domain), TAF(II)28, TAF(II)42, TAF(II)62, TAF(II)135 (histone fold domain), Chrac-14, Chrac-16, NC2 alpha and NC2 beta, NF-Y subunit beta (Nf-Yb3) and NF-Y subunit gamma (Nf-Yc2), the Histone domain of Son of sevenless protein (sunid 101107; homology_scope 'dm', no warnings), and an automated-matches node (194413).
- a.22.1.4 Bacterial histone-fold protein (sunid 101318).
- a.22.1.0 automated matches (sunid 238448), an automated placement node rather than a curated family.

SCOPe level interpretation: histones (a.22.1.1) and the TAF/NC2/NF-Y and Son of sevenless histone-fold domains (a.22.1.3), and the archaeal and bacterial histone-fold families (a.22.1.2, a.22.1.4), are all in one superfamily. SCOPe therefore asserts probable common ancestry for the histone-fold domains at the superfamily level only; the closest family-level relationship is within a.22.1.1 (core histones and macro-H2A.1), and the TAF-type members form a separate family, a.22.1.3, that SCOPe places as more distant from core histones within the same superfamily. Name-only matches are not histone-fold relatives: the histone H1 and H5 globular domains (sunids 46830, 46828) carry SCCS a.4.5.13, a different superfamily in class a, and the histone-named methyltransferases and deacetylases (Dot1l c.66.1.31, SET7/9 b.85.7.1 and b.76.2.1, p300 d.108.1.11, HDAC7/8 c.42.1.2) and the H3 C-terminal fragment (j.63.1.1) are classified in other folds or classes. SCOPe makes no homology claim between these and the histone-fold superfamily, and that absence of a claim is not a proof of non-homology.

Limits: (1) Only release 2.08 was queried; the periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16 was not checked, so current-periodic status is unverified. (2) Family membership is SCOPe classification, not a functional assignment; the nucleosome-forming role of core histones is not transferred to TAFs, NC2, NF-Y or the Son of sevenless domain, and no function was inferred. (3) The search for 'histone' was a single page of 20 hits with has_more=true, so it is a bounded window; the family listings used for a.22.1.1, a.22.1.3 and the superfamily are complete (has_more=false), but the members of a.22.1.2 and a.22.1.4 were not enumerated beyond the search hits and the family nodes. (4) No sequence or FATCAT hits, structure alignments, or AlphaFold evidence were retrieved, so no structural or remote-homology claim beyond SCOPe placement is made here.

Because the two domains sit in different families, SCOPe makes no closer (family-level) claim. Functional conclusions that go beyond this evidence: (1) Do not infer that the MazG-like domain has the HisE-type activity (phosphoribosyl-ATP pyrophosphatase) or takes part in histidine biosynthesis. (5) Absence of a family-level link is not a negative homology claim, and the distinct-family placement is not evidence that they are unrelated or convergent.

The family nodes I retrieved carry no warnings, heterogeneity, repeats, or inconsistencies.

Interpretation: the three should be read as separate families inside one homologous superfamily. SCOPe does not place them in a shared family, so the closest verified relationship is at the superfamily level, and the family split records divergence within that shared architecture. The chemical differences between them do not contradict SCOPe's placement; they are what functional divergence within a superfamily looks like. A shared superfamily supports common ancestry but not shared biochemistry, so the superfamily placement alone cannot say that any member performs any particular reaction.

Limits: the enzymatic and storage chemistries (iron storage and oxidation for ferritin, radical generation for RNR R2, and H2O2 dismutation for Mn catalase) are background knowledge. SCOPe returned no reaction, substrate, or mechanism annotation for these families, so they are not verified here and should not be inferred for any member from its placement. SCOPe gives no order of divergence and no sequence or structural basis for it. I retrieved no sequence or structure alignment between these families, and I did not run domain-level BLAST or FATCAT comparisons or check domain-level representatives beyond search hits. A name search for 'ribonucleotide reductase' returned no results, so the RNR-like placement came from the superfamily's child listing rather than from a name match. These families should not be called analogs, convergent, or nonhomologous; the verified SCOPe position is superfamily-level homology. To go further, one would need a same-release domain lineage comparison of representative ferritin, RNR-like, and Mn catalase domains, plus sequence or structure alignments and primary literature for the bimetal-site residues and the mechanistic claims.

prompt: Plastocyanin/azurin-like proteins, ephrin ectodomains, and the N-terminal domain of PAD4 appear biologically unrelated. What does SCOPe say about their relationship, and should copper binding or electron transfer be inferred across them?
answer:
Verified SCOPe facts (release 2.08): all three are in one superfamily. Plastocyanin/azurin-like (sunid 49504, b.6.1.1), Ephrin ectodomain (sunid 74874, b.6.1.5) and Peptidylarginine deiminase Pad4 N-terminal domain (sunid 110107, b.6.1.6) each have parent Cupredoxins superfamily b.6.1 (sunid 49503), which sits in the Cupredoxin-like fold b.6 (sunid 49502) and the all-beta class b. The superfamily node carries the annotation 'contains copper-binding site' and implies homology at superfamily scope with no warnings. The ephrin ectodomain family is annotated as a eukaryotic signaling domain 'probably related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site'; the PAD4 N-terminal family is annotated 'probably related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site'. The plastocyanin/azurin-like family record has only 'mono-domain proteins' and no copper comment of its own.

Interpretation: SCOPe does not treat these three as biologically unrelated. It places them in one superfamily, which is a positive assertion of probable common ancestry at the cupredoxin-like core, with the two non-plastocyanin families hedged as 'probably related'. The three families are distinct, so the shared relationship is superfamily-level only and does not make them one family. Shared superfamily membership is not a claim about shared biochemistry, so it does not transfer function.

Copper binding: do not infer it for the ephrin ectodomains or the PAD4 N-terminal domain. Their SCOPe family annotations explicitly say they lack the metal-binding site. The copper-site statement applies at superfamily level, and the copper-binding role of plastocyanin/azurin is background knowledge, not something this SCOPe record shows for those families.

Electron transfer: SCOPe asserts nothing about electron transfer for any of the three, so it should not be inferred across them. Ephrin ectodomains are annotated as a signaling domain, and nothing retrieved links the PAD4 N-terminal domain to deimination activity. That catalytic activity sits in the separate catalytic domain (d.126.1.5, sunid 111153), and the middle domain is b.2.9.1 (sunid 110084). Only the N-terminal domain is in the cupredoxin-like fold, so the placement must not be generalized to whole PAD4. Also, ephrin receptors are in different folds (b.1.2.1, b.18.1.4), so the term 'ephrin' alone is not enough; the ligand ectodomain is the b.6.1.5 family.

Limits: I retrieved family and superfamily nodes, not domain-level records or sequences for specific PDB entries. I did not run a sequence or structure comparison between these families and did not check any function literature, so the superfamily-level ancestry rests on SCOPe's hierarchy and its hedged annotations alone. The results come from the 2.08 release as returned by the service.

Limits: the API gives no rationale for the split. The only b.84.5 annotation is PubMed 19893485, given as an ID only; I did not retrieve the paper, so the reason for the split is unverified. The Thermus domain carries the record annotation 'complexed with adp'; that does not establish the bulge domain's function, catalytic role, or rotary mechanism. The other V1 A-subunit domains are separate SCOPe nodes in other folds (b.49.1.2 'V1 ATP synthase A subunit, domain 1' and a.69.1.2 'C-terminal domain'), known here only from search output, so the bulge classification does not describe the whole A subunit.

Under the skill's rules, a shared fold is structural similarity, not common ancestry. Because the three groups are in different superfamilies, SCOPe makes no positive superfamily-level homology claim among them. Limits: I used release 2.08 (the stable label; the service also lists a 2.08-2026-08-16 periodic update, which I did not query separately). No warnings or heterogeneity flags were returned for any of the four nodes. The c.2.1.1 annotation says 'N-terminal all-beta domain defines family', so its family placement rests on a feature I did not check against a domain sequence or boundary. Interpretation: a biologist should read this as one ancient dinucleotide-binding Rossmann-type module that diverged into several functionally distinct families (alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal, CoA-binding, and potassium-channel NAD-binding). The shared superfamily supports probable common ancestry of the Rossmann-type core, not a shared substrate, cofactor role, or catalytic activity. The family names are the only functional labels I retrieved; they should not be turned into a claim that the three families bind the same ligand or perform the same reaction. Limits: I did not retrieve domain SIDs, endpoints, sequences, BLAST or FATCAT hits, or structures for these families, so this answer makes no claim about specific proteins, boundaries, or residue-level conservation. Natural-language name searches for the three families returned no hits; I found them by browsing the children of c.2.1 instead. Any transfer of function, ligand, or structural template from one family to another needs family-specific experimental or structural evidence that SCOPe does not provide here.

prompt: Andreeva et al. 2008 describe PA1492 as a classification-change example. How did the relationship between PA1492 (PDB 1t1j) and nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase (PDB 1f8y) change between SCOP 1.69 and the current SCOPe release?
answer:
Short answer: PA1492 (1t1j chain A) moved from a different fold into the same superfamily as nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase (1f8y). SCOPe 1.69 placed it in fold c.137; SCOPe 2.08, the current public release reported by the service, places it in superfamily c.23.14 with 1f8y.

Verified SCOPe facts (each release queried separately):
- Release 1.69: 1t1j chain A is domain d1t1ja_ (sunid 106249), classified c.137.1.1 'Hypothetical protein PA1492'. Lineage: class c (a/b) > fold c.137 (sunid 110459) > superfamily c.137.1 (sunid 110460) > family c.137.1.1 (sunid 110461). 1f8y chain A is d1f8ya_ (sunid 31395), classified c.23.14.1 'Nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase' (Lactobacillus leichmannii), lineage class c > fold c.23 (flavodoxin-like) > superfamily c.23.14 (named 'N-deoxyribosyltransferase' in 1.69) > family c.23.14.1 (sunid 52310).
- Release 2.08: the same sunid 106249 is now domain d1t1ja1 (description '1t1j A:1-118'), classified c.23.14.2 'Hypothetical protein PA1492', lineage class c > fold c.23 > superfamily c.23.14 (sunid 52309, renamed 'N-(deoxy)ribosyltransferase-like') > family c.23.14.2 (sunid 110461). d1f8ya_ remains c.23.14.1 in the same superfamily.

Change: PA1492 went from fold c.137 (no shared superfamily with 1f8y) to superfamily c.23.14, shared with nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase. Its family is different from 1f8y's (c.23.14.2 vs c.23.14.1). The homology flags for both 2.08 domains show homology_implied_by_level true and no warnings. At the superfamily level SCOPe therefore asserts probable common ancestry between PA1492 and the 1f8y family. Family-level sharing is not asserted.

Limits:
- The lookup was by sunid 106249. The 1.69 SID d1t1ja_ and the 2.08 SID d1t1ja1 differ, and d1t1ja1 returned not-found in 1.69, so the link across releases rests on the shared sunid.
- SCOPe placement does not establish substrate, catalytic activity, or mechanism for PA1492. Its family name remains 'Hypothetical protein' in both releases, and nothing retrieved assigns it nucleoside-processing function.
- I did not retrieve the Andreeva et al. 2008 paper or any sequence/structure alignment. The reason SCOPe moved PA1492 (structural, sequence, or literature) is therefore unverified; the API shows only the change.
- I queried release 2.08 as the current public release. The latest periodic update label (2.08-2026-08-16) was not queried separately.
- The 2.08 entry for 1t1j also carries two short l.1.1.1 domain records (d1t1ja2, d1t1jb2) absent from 1.69. I did not evaluate them and they do not change the d1t1ja1 classification.

prompt: How did the SCOP 1.75 domain definitions for PDB 1acc chain A change in newer releases of SCOPe? What does the change reveal about domains as evolutionary modules, and how should it affect homology searches?
answer:
Verified SCOPe facts. SCOP 1.75 and SCOPe 2.08 (the stable release, queried separately) disagree on how chain 1accA (anthrax protective antigen, UniProt P13423, 735 residues) is divided into domains.

Release 1.75: the chain has one classified domain, d1acca_, with description '1acc A:' and no endpoints returned. It is SCCS f.11.1.1 ('Anthrax protective antigen', fold f.11, superfamily f.11.1, class f). Its returned genetic SEQRES domain sequence is 722 residues. That length matches chain residues 14-735, and the sequence begins SSSQGLL, which is the same start as the 2.08 N-terminal domain. The 1.75 endpoints are therefore inferred from sequence, not returned by the API.

Release 2.08: the chain has two domains. d1acca2 is A:14-225, b.179.1.1 (PA14, fold b.179 'Anthrax protective antigen N-terminal-like', class b), 212 residues. d1acca1 is A:226-735, f.60.1.1 ('Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like', fold f.60, class f), 510 residues. Their sequences tile the 1.75 region exactly (212 + 510 = 722): the 1.75 domain sequence is d1acca2 followed by d1acca1. Both 2.08 domains carry the annotation 'complexed with ca' and have empty heterogeneity and warning lists, as does the 1.75 domain's homology record. The 2.08 chain record names 3tewA as its cluster representative (96.9% local sequence identity). That is a comparison link only and does not transfer any classification to 1accA.

Interpretation. The change is a split of one domain into two, placed in different folds and classes. The 1.75 label f.11.1.1 is gone from this chain in 2.08; the N-terminal module is now b.179.1.1 and the C-terminal module f.60.1.1. Because SCOPe classifies domains rather than whole chains, the same 722-residue region was one evolutionary unit in 1.75 and is two classified modules in 2.08. A chain-level family or superfamily label is therefore a release-specific assertion about one module, and it changes when the domain partition changes. In 2.08, SCOPe makes no positive homology assertion between the PA14-like N-terminal module and the f.60 C-terminal module. That does not establish that they are unrelated, analogous, or convergent. The retrieved data do not give the structural, sequence, or literature rationale for the split, so I cannot say why SCOPe made it.

Homology-search implications. Use 2.08 domain boundaries for new work. Do not attach the 1.75 label f.11.1.1 to the whole chain as a current classification. Evaluate any sequence or structure hit to 1accA by its aligned range, and check each range separately against d1acca2 (14-225) and d1acca1 (226-735). A hit that supports one module does not establish homology for the other. A hit to the 1.75-era whole-chain domain should be read as supporting the combined region only if its range covers both modules. Historical 1.75 records are archived classifications, not the current domain inventory.

Limits. Only 1.75 and the stable 2.08 were queried. The 2.08 periodic update (2.08-2026-08-16) appears in current-release metadata, but I did not retrieve its records, and I did not check intermediate releases. So I cannot say when the split happened, and 'newer releases' is answered only for 2.08-stable. No BLAST or FATCAT hits were retrieved, so there is no hit-based homology evidence here. No function, ligand, or mechanism is established by these records beyond the 'complexed with ca' annotation and the protein name. The 2.08 domain-sequence ranges were checked by sequence matching against the 1.75 sequence, not by a residue mapping from the API.

prompt: What does SCOPe's five-domain decomposition of Prp8 in PDB 3jb9 reveal about its evolutionary history? Which domains are related to previously characterized proteins, and which represents a newly observed fold?
answer:
Verified SCOPe facts (release 2.08; the current release reports 2.08 as its stable label). PDB 3jb9 chain A is Prp8: its SCOPe chain record links UniProt O14187 and a 2363-residue SEQRES, and its lineages name 'Pre-mRNA splicing factor 8, Prp8 / Spp42'. The five chain-A domains are:
- d3jb9a5 (A:47-697), d.394.1.1, N-terminal domain of Prp8/Spp42.
- d3jb9a4 (A:698-822), a.29.2.1, Bromodomain family (fold a.29, Bromodomain-like).
- d3jb9a3 (A:823-1604), e.8.1.8, Splicing factor Prp8 RT domain (superfamily e.8.1, DNA/RNA polymerases).
- d3jb9a2 (A:1605-1780), c.52.1.36, Splicing factor Prp8 endonuclease-like domain (superfamily c.52.1, restriction endonuclease-like).
- d3jb9a1 (A:1784-2030), c.55.3.14, Prp8 beta-finger domain-like family (superfamily c.55.3, Ribonuclease H-like).
All five have empty homology warnings and no repeat or inconsistency annotations in 2.08.

Interpretation. The mosaic spans four previously classified folds (a.29, c.52, c.55 and e.8, the last as superfamily e.8.1) plus one Prp8-specific fold, d.394. The closest tie to a previously characterized family is d3jb9a4, placed in the existing Bromodomain family (a.29.2.1). Domains d3jb9a1, a2 and a3 are placed in existing superfamilies (c.55.3, c.52.1, e.8.1), so SCOPe asserts homology only at superfamily level for them. The newly observed fold is d3jb9a5 (d.394, SUNID 345891). d.394 is absent from releases 1.75 and 2.06 and present in 2.07 and 2.08, so within the releases I queried it is the new fold. The Prp8 beta-finger family (SUNID 159638) and protein node (159639) were already present in 1.75, so that part of Prp8's classification is long-established.

Limits. (1) The 'related to' statements rest on SCOPe placement. I did not retrieve other members of the four superfamilies or the bromodomain family, and I ran no sequence or structure comparison of my own, so this is SCOPe's assertion, not independent evidence. (2) SCOPe's homology is not functional transfer: nothing here establishes endonuclease, reverse-transcriptase, bromodomain/acetyl-lysine-binding or other catalytic or ligand activity. (3) 'Newly observed' means first appearing in SCOPe among the releases checked (1.75, 2.06, 2.07, 2.08). I did not check intermediate releases, and absence from SCOPe does not show the fold has no relatives outside SCOPe; SCOPe makes no positive homology claim for d.394 to any other fold. (4) Historical SCCS codes were not treated as stable identities across releases; I relied on the SUNID lineages I retrieved. (5) The five domains cover only residues 47-2030 of the 2363-residue chain; residues 1-46 and 2031-2363 have no domain in 2.08. (6) The PDB summary says 'yeast spliceosome', and the domain species labels say S. pombe 972h-; I did not resolve the species beyond what SCOPe records. (7) I retrieved no BLAST or FATCAT hits for 3jb9A, so no structure-led or sequence-led evidence is included.

prompt: Why do d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, and d4cj9a_ all belong to TAL effector family a.298.1.1 in SCOPe despite vastly different sequence lengths?
answer:
Short answer: SCOPe places all three in family a.298.1.1 because they share the TAL-effector repeat architecture, and the family is defined by that repeated unit, not by the total domain length. The lengths differ because the number of repeat units differs, and SCOPe's own annotations say so.

Verified SCOPe facts (release 2.08):
- Lineage for all three is identical through the family: class a (All alpha proteins), fold a.298 (Left-handed alpha-alpha superhelix), superfamily a.298.1 (TAL effector-like), family a.298.1.1 (TAL (transcription activator-like) effector). Protein-level names differ: d2kq5a_ = PthA (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri), d3v6pa_ = dHax3 (Xanthomonas, TaxId 338), d4cj9a_ = BurrH (Burkholderia rhizoxinica). These are SCOPe hierarchy levels, not external taxonomy records.
- Genetic SEQRES domain lengths retrieved: d2kq5a_ = 51 residues; d3v6pa_ = 373; d4cj9a_ = 752. The length spread is therefore real in this release.
- d2kq5a_ carries the comment 'single repeat'. All three carry a 're' heterogeneity note: it applies to all domains of a family whose common domain is composed of a different number of small repeating units.
- The family repeat annotation gives 4cj9 A:259-292 as the canonical representative repeat, a 34-residue span (292-259+1). Its coordinates apply to d4cj9a_ itself; the API marks them as not applying to d2kq5a_ or d3v6pa_ (coordinates_apply_to_requested_node = false). Homology is implied by the family level (homology_scope px, no warnings).

Interpretation: The family-level placement rests on the shared tandem repeat module, which SCOPe treats as the homology-bearing element at family level. Domain length tracks how many modules a given protein carries. Using the 34-residue canonical span as a rough unit, d2kq5a_ (51 residues) is about 1.5 units, consistent with its 'single repeat' comment; d3v6pa_ (373) is about 11 units and d4cj9a_ (752) at most about 22 units, counting its flanks. These unit counts are my arithmetic, not API values. The 're' note is the curated signal that SCOPe keeps a family together despite a varying repeat count.

Limits:
- The API shows the classification and the repeat note but not the curators' sequence or structural rationale for grouping these three. That rationale was not verified from the retrieved data.
- The repeat-unit boundaries for d2kq5a_ and d3v6pa_ were not retrieved; the 4cj9 A:259-292 coordinates must not be transferred to them.
- The 752-residue d4cj9a_ domain includes sequence beyond the annotated repeat span; its flank boundaries were not verified.
- Family membership does not establish DNA-binding specificity, repeat-variable residue function, or any substrate. Those claims need literature or experimental evidence, which was not consulted here.
- No quality (SPACI/AEROSPACI) or structure-hit evidence was retrieved, so no representative or structure ranking is made.
- No historical reclassification was checked; the statement is limited to release 2.08.

answer: The current-release metadata reports SCOPe release 2.08 as the stable release, with stable_label "2.08-stable" (release_date 2021-09-22, freeze_date 2021-07-28, is_public true, is_comprehensive false). The latest periodic update is reported as version "2.08-2026-08-16", dated 2026-08-16, and the current-release api_url is /api/v1/releases/2.08. For a reproducible analysis, cite and pin the stable release: SCOPe 2.08 ("2.08-stable"), and pass release=2.08 on every call. prompt: Early structures 1br0 and 1ez3 contained fragments of the syntaxin N-terminal domain, whereas 1dn1 chain B showed the full domain. How should SCOPe's current treatment of these structures change the biological interpretation of fragment-based fold assignments?
answer:
In SCOPe 2.08, the fragment structures are not reclassified out of the fold or family. What changes is the annotation caveat that governs how their fold assignments should be read.

Verified facts (release 2.08, the current public release per service info): d1br0a_ (1br0 chain A) and d1ez3a_, d1ez3b_, d1ez3c_ (1ez3 chains A, B, C) are all a.47.2.1: class a (all alpha), fold a.47 (STAT-like), superfamily a.47.2 (t-snare proteins), family a.47.2.1 (t-snare proteins), protein 'Syntaxin 1A N-terminal domain'. Each carries the comment 'three-helical fragment; similar to one spectrin repeat' and an 'ms' inconsistency flag (missing some secondary structures, under one-third of the common domain). No homology warnings are returned. The genetic sequence of d1br0a_ is 120 residues. d1dn1b_ (1dn1 chain B) has the same a.47.2.1 lineage, but no fragment comment and no 'ms' flag. Its annotation is 'automated match to d3c98b_', and its protein-level parent is the 'automated matches' node. Its sequence is 222 residues; the first 120 residues are identical to d1br0a_ except the penultimate residue (S versus C). The 1dn1 PDB entry is marked obsolete, obsoleted by 3c98 (obsolete date 2008-03-25).

Interpretation: the fragment-based assignments should be read as partial-domain evidence for the same a.47.2.1 family, not as a separate or conflicting fold call. The fold and family placement is retained. The change is in completeness: 1br0 and 1ez3 cover the N-terminal helical portion, and 1dn1 chain B's domain extends beyond it. A fragment-based fold call therefore supports the placement of that N-terminal region but does not establish the full domain's boundaries or the structure of the remaining residues. If 1dn1 chain B is used as the full-domain reference, note that its classification rests on an automated match and its entry is obsolete. The replacement 3c98 was not retrieved and should be checked before use.

Limits: (1) The 'spectrin repeat' remark is an annotation comment about similarity, not a SCOPe homology assertion. Do not infer spectrin homology or shared function from it. (2) The absence of a fragment flag on 1dn1 chain B is an absence of warning, not positive proof of completeness; I did not check its boundaries against other sources. (3) The premise that SCOPe reclassified these structures is not supported by the 2.08 data. I did not query earlier releases, so I cannot say whether a reclassification occurred or why the fragments were retained. The 2.08 record shows retention with an annotation caveat, and the rationale for that is unverified. (4) I queried release 2.08 and did not check the 2026-08-16 periodic update. No quality measures were retrieved, so no structural-quality ranking is made. (5) The 1dn1 chain A partner (d1dn1a_, sccs e.25.1.1) was not evaluated and is outside this question. (6) Nothing here establishes the N-terminal domain's functional role in SNARE assembly or regulation.

prompt: NAD(P)-binding enzymes occur in multiple SCOP folds and superfamilies. What does this imply about convergent versus divergent evolution, and why is cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone insufficient evidence of homology?
answer:
Verified SCOPe 2.08 facts: the NAD(P)-binding description occurs under two different folds in class c. Fold c.2 is "NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains" (sunid 51734), with one child superfamily, c.2.1 (sunid 51735), of the same description. Fold c.3 is "FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain" (sunid 51904), with one child superfamily, c.3.1 (sunid 51905), of the same description. Both folds sit under class c (sunid 51349). Only these two folds were retrieved; a search for the cofactor-binding phrase returned no results, so this is not a complete inventory of NAD(P)-binding folds in SCOPe.

Interpretation: SCOPe places the two cofactor-binding groups in different folds, so SCOPe asserts no fold-level or superfamily-level common ancestry between them. That placement is not a proof of convergence or of independent origin. Hierarchy placement is a positive homology claim only when shared; its absence is not a negative evolutionary claim. Within c.2, the Rossmann-type superfamily is the only one recorded in 2.08, so this release records no alternative superfamily under that fold. I did not retrieve families (for example c.2.1.x) or domain members, so I cannot say from these data whether the superfamily diversified divergently into families.

Why cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone is insufficient: a dinucleotide-binding site is a functional constraint. Unrelated or distantly related proteins can converge on similar cofactor-contact geometry, and a shared site can persist after the rest of the fold has diverged. Homology needs evidence that the proteins descend from a common ancestor, normally shared lineage at family or superfamily level in SCOPe, supported by sequence or structural evidence beyond the ligand contact. Fold-level structural similarity also does not establish common ancestry. From pretrained knowledge, not from these API responses: a Rossmann-like dinucleotide-binding motif is a recurring chemical solution, which is one reason it can arise more than once.

Limits: the claim is limited to SCOPe release 2.08 and the two retrieved folds. The API data do not establish the cofactor identity (NAD versus NADP) for any domain, a specific substrate, reaction, or function, or the relationship between any particular pair of domains. A pairwise homology statement would require both domain lineages retrieved in the same release, which I did not do. No homology or annotation warnings were retrieved for these nodes. A quality ranking was not requested and was not performed.

prompt: How did the relationship between the ColG collagenase domain in PDB 1nqd and the Cry3A C-terminal domain in PDB 1dlc change from SCOPe 2.04 to current SCOPe, and what structural and functional evidence supports their common ancestry?
answer:
Verified SCOPe facts (2.04 vs. 2.08; the service reports 2.08 as the current public stable release):
- 1nqd, SCOPe 2.04: chain A (d1nqda_, SUNID 86025) and chain B (d1nqdb_, SUNID 86026) were both b.23.2.1, Collagen-binding domain, in superfamily b.23.2 and CUB-like fold b.23.
- 1nqd, SCOPe 2.08: chain A (d1nqda_, same SUNID 86025) is b.18.1.36, Collagen-binding domain family, in superfamily b.18.1 (Galactose-binding domain-like) and fold b.18. Chain B was split: d1nqdb1 (B:893-1008, SUNID 86026) is b.18.1.36, and d1nqdb2 (B:891-892, SUNID 281794) is an l.1.1.1 tag artifact with an artifact_not_homology_evidence warning. The protein is Class 1 collagenase from C. histolyticum.
- 1dlc, both releases: chain A C-terminal domain d1dlca1 (A:500-644, SUNID 23719) is b.18.1.3, delta-Endotoxin C-terminal domain, in superfamily b.18.1 and fold b.18 (CRYIIIA, B. thuringiensis tenebrionis). Its classification did not change between 2.04 and 2.08.

What changed: the ColG collagen-binding domain (SCOPe classifies it as the CBD, not the catalytic collagenase domain) moved from fold b.23 (CUB-like) to fold b.18 (Galactose-binding domain-like) and superfamily b.18.1. Before 2.08, the CBD and the Cry3A C-terminal domain were in different folds, so SCOPe made no shared-level claim. In 2.08 they share superfamily b.18.1 but not family (b.18.1.36 vs. b.18.1.3). The API records the reclassification only. It does not give a reason, and it does not show the PDB revision change (selected_pdb_release revision date 2009-02-24 in 2.04, 2019-07-24 in 2.08) as the cause.

Interpretation: under SCOPe 2.08, the shared superfamily b.18.1 is an official SCOPe placement that supports probable common ancestry at the superfamily level only. It does not support a shared family, and it does not establish shared function. The collagen-binding and Cry-toxin receptor-binding roles are background from model knowledge; no retrieved record states them as shared function, so they are unverified here.

Structural evidence actually retrieved (structure-led, non-official):
- No direct 1nqd-to-1dlc hit was retrieved. 1nqdA returned no sequence or structure hits. Its cluster representative 1nqjA (99.2% identity) returned 50 structure hits with p <= 0.0096 and has_more=true; d1dlca1 was not in that window. The only b.18.1.3 hit there was d1w99a3 (Cry4Ba C-terminal domain, p=0.0040, RMSD 2.52 A, 2.5% identity), which is weak and representative-based. The b.18.1.36 self-family hit d5ikua1 (automated match to d1nqda_, p=4e-14, RMSD 1.72, 28.7% identity) supports family consistency only.
- 1dlcA's C-terminal region (chain start ~500-509) matches other b.18.1 members: d2qkga3 (b.18.1.0, p=3e-5, RMSD 1.42, 35% identity), d1w99a3 (b.18.1.3, p=2e-4, RMSD 1.43, 25.8%), d1ux7a_ (b.18.1.28 xylanase, p=0.0075, RMSD 2.37), and d1w9wa_ (b.18.1.10, p=0.0076, RMSD 1.58). Sequence hits to the same region are Cry-to-Cry (d1ji6a1 and d1ciya1, 17-19% identity). None of these is a CBD match.
- Hit streams give no residue correspondence, so the 1nqd and 1dlc regions cannot be mapped to each other.

Limits: 'current' is 2.08 as reported; the periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16 was not queried separately. A limit-100 structure-hit retrieval for 1nqjA exceeded output limits, and I did not read the spilled file because it is outside the workspace. The hit window for 1nqjA is therefore bounded at 50 and unresolved beyond it. No quality, alignment, or literature source was retrieved to explain the 2.08 reassignment.

prompt: d1p7jd_ and d1ztra1 share homeodomain family a.4.1.1, but d1ztra1 has an hf annotation. What remains justified about homology, and why should the structures not be treated as interchangeable templates or training examples?
answer:
Verified in SCOPe release 2.08 (current): d1p7jd_ (sunid 94286) and d1ztra1 (sunid 125655) share the full lineage class a (All alpha proteins), fold a.4 (DNA/RNA-binding 3-helical bundle), superfamily a.4.1 (Homeodomain-like), and family a.4.1.1 (Homeodomain). Both are assigned to the same protein entry, Engrailed homeodomain from Drosophila melanogaster. Both homology records report homology_implied_by_level=true at domain (px) scope with no warnings. Only d1ztra1 carries an hf (heterogeneous fold) inconsistency, at domain scope and not inherited. SCOPe describes hf as applying to domains that adopt a different fold than the exemplar domain but have similar sequence and number of secondary structures. Both records also carry a 'mutant' comment (d1p7jd_ additionally 'complexed with nhe; mutant').

What remains justified: SCOPe's family-level placement, which is a positive classification-level assertion that the two domains share ancestry as members of family a.4.1.1. The hf note does not withdraw that assertion; it is a caveat on the structure of d1ztra1. The note itself states that d1ztra1 has similar sequence and secondary-structure count to the family, but I did not retrieve sequence or structure hits, so I cannot quantify their identity or structural similarity beyond what SCOPe states. The family placement also does not, by itself, establish a particular function for either domain.

Why they should not be treated as interchangeable templates: the hf flag says d1ztra1 adopts a different fold from the family exemplar. A shared family therefore does not establish a shared three-dimensional conformation for this domain, so the family placement cannot justify using d1ztra1 as a structural template for d1p7jd_ or the reverse. The exemplar domain is not identified in the retrieved data, and I did not retrieve FATCAT alignments or residue mappings, so the nature and extent of the fold difference are unverified.

Why they should not be treated as interchangeable training examples: they share a family label but carry conflicting structural meaning. A family-level label would assign both the same classification, while the hf flag marks d1ztra1 as an exception for fold-level labels. Any family-grouped split should keep the two domains in the same partition, since SCOPe places them in the same family. Any fold-level or structure-based target should either use the hf status explicitly or hold d1ztra1 out pending review. Both records are mutant structures, so mutation status should also be considered before treating either as a wild-type exemplar.

Limits: this answer relies only on SCOPe classification, annotation, and homology-warning records for the two domains in release 2.08. It does not establish sequence identity, the fold difference's structural basis, the function of either domain, or the exemplar's identity. Those would need sequence or structure hit records for d1ztra1 and the family exemplar's record, which were not retrieved here.

prompt: d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 belong to fibronectin type III family b.1.2.1, but d1o5dt2 is annotated as a fragment. How should that annotation affect alignment, representative selection, and interpretation of family diversity?
answer:
Verified in SCOPe release 2.08: d1uc6a1 (sunid 107766, 1uc6 A:6-109, protein entry 'Ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor alpha', human) and d1o5dt2 (sunid 103884, 1o5d T:107-205, protein entry 'Extracellular region of human tissue factor', human) both have lineage class b > fold b.1 > superfamily b.1.2 > family b.1.2.1 (Fibronectin type III). d1o5dt2 carries a 'fr' annotation (fragment; missing more than one-third of the common structure and/or sequence). It is set on the domain itself, not inherited, and is the only heterogeneity entry in its homology section, which has no warnings. It also has a comment 'complexed with cr9'; I did not retrieve what CR9 is. d1uc6a1 has no annotations or heterogeneity flags.

Alignment: treat d1o5dt2 as a partial member. Any alignment to it should report the aligned range, and the uncovered portion should be marked as not observed rather than read as sequence or structural divergence. Do not compute full-length identity or coverage against it as if it were complete. The API gives no map of which third is missing, so the missing region is unverified. Its 107-205 coordinates are PDB numbering, so mapping them onto a sequence alignment needs a verified residue mapping.

Representative selection: the fragment flag is a reason not to pick d1o5dt2 as the family representative when a non-fragment member of comparable quality exists. It is not a quality ranking. I did not retrieve SPACI/AEROSPACI or resolution for either entry, nor the full b.1.2.1 membership, so I cannot say d1uc6a1 is the best representative. Before choosing, retrieve quality for every candidate and list the non-fragment members.

Family diversity: both domains share family b.1.2.1 in the same release, so SCOPe supports a family-level relationship between them. The fragment flag does not change that placement; it limits how much of d1o5dt2's common structure is observed. Counting d1o5dt2 adds one protein-level entry (CNTF receptor alpha versus tissue factor extracellular region) but only partial structural coverage, so it should not be weighted as full-length evidence for the family's structural diversity. The protein-level labels are SCOPe hierarchy entries, not functional claims. I retrieved no function or ligand evidence, so I cannot say the two proteins share function or that CR9 binding is shared.

Limits: not established from the retrieved data are the actual missing region of d1o5dt2, any sequence or structure alignment, quality metrics, the complete family membership, whether other b.1.2.1 members are fragments, and any historical reclassification. The homology section reports homology implied at the domain level for both entries, but that does not license transferring function or a specific template. Next checks: list the children of family sunid 49266 to get full membership and their annotations, then retrieve SPACI/AEROSPACI for the candidate representatives.

prompt: A newly solved domain resembles a known SCOPe fold but lacks convincing evidence of common ancestry with any existing superfamily. Should it be assigned to a new family, a new superfamily in the existing fold, or a new fold? What biological claim does each choice make?
answer:
Recommendation: place the domain as a new superfamily within the existing fold, but only after structural inspection confirms that its topology matches that fold. Do not place it in a family. If the topology does not match on inspection, make it a new fold. Verified context (SCOPe 2.08): fold a.1 is Globin-like (sunid 46457), its child superfamily a.1.1 is also Globin-like (sunid 46458), and the fold annotation reads 'core: 6 helices; folded leaf, partly opened'. The homology endpoint for the fold warns that SCOPe levels above superfamily do not imply homology.

What each choice claims:
(1) New family: asserts close evolutionary relationship, meaning common ancestry with an existing superfamily at family resolution. That contradicts the premise, which has no convincing ancestry evidence with any superfamily, so this choice is unsupported.
(2) New superfamily in the existing fold: makes a structural claim that the domain shares the fold's major secondary-structure content, arrangement and connectivity. It also makes an evolutionary claim restricted to the new group: its members are asserted to share probable common ancestry. It does not assert ancestry with the other superfamilies in that fold, and it does not claim they are unrelated or convergent. SCOPe's choice of superfamily is the absence of a positive homology assertion, not evidence of a negative one. The group needs member-level evidence (more than one related sequence or structure, or shared motifs beyond the fold). A singleton is a weak basis for a superfamily.
(3) New fold: claims the topology does not match any existing fold at SCOPe's structural threshold. It is a purely structural claim and says nothing about ancestry.

Decision rule: a resemblance strong enough to call it 'resembles a known fold' is what decides between (2) and (3). Use (2) if the alignment shows the same topology and connectivity. Use (3) if the resemblance is only generic (for example, a generic helix bundle) or if the topology fails on inspection. Any later evidence of common ancestry with a specific superfamily would move the domain there, possibly at family level.

Limits: no domain sequence or coordinates were supplied, so no FATCAT or BLAST hits were retrieved and no alignment or topology was inspected. This answer is a conditional decision rule, not a classification of a specific domain. An absence of sequence hits does not prove the absence of homology. Any result from this analysis is a non-official candidate hypothesis and must be verified by FATCAT P-value, score and RMSD, competing lineages, residue mapping, and topology inspection before it is treated as more than a candidate.

prompt: Canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases have related catalytic-domain architecture in SCOPe. What common evolutionary or mechanistic conclusions are justified, and what evidence is needed before transferring substrate specificity or regulation?
answer:
Verified SCOPe facts (release 2.08, the stable release; the service also lists a periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16, which I did not query): canonical protein kinases (d.144.1.7, 'Protein kinases, catalytic subunit', sunid 88854), APH phosphotransferases (d.144.1.6, sunid 64411), and the PI3K catalytic domain (d.144.1.4, sunid 56171) are three separate families inside superfamily d.144.1 'Protein kinase-like (PK-like)' (sunid 56112), fold d.144, class d (alpha+beta). The superfamily homology record reports homology implied by level, scope sf, with no warnings or heterogeneity; each of the three family records reports homology implied at family scope with no warnings. The superfamily annotation comment says the fold 'shares functional and structural similarities with the ATP-grasp fold and PIPK.' That is a curated comment, not a SCOPe homology assertion, and I did not retrieve the ATP-grasp or PIPK records, so I cannot classify them. The protein-kinase family annotation only says members are organized into groups and subfamilies; no detail was returned. The search for 'protein kinase-like' returned no results, so I relied on the direct identifier lookup instead.

Interpretation: Because the three families share superfamily d.144.1, SCOPe asserts probable common ancestry of the PK-like catalytic core at superfamily level. That is the deepest level at which SCOPe justifies a shared evolutionary conclusion for these three named groups, and it supports a shared core architecture. Shared phosphotransfer chemistry is general biochemical background from model memory, not SCOPe-verified: these enzymes move a phosphoryl group to different acceptors (protein residues, aminoglycosides, phosphoinositides). The separate family assignments mean SCOPe does not place them in one family, so family-level substrate recognition should not be treated as shared.

Limits: The superfamily placement does not establish identical substrate specificity, catalytic-residue identity, regulatory mechanism, or interchangeable inhibitors or structural templates. Family placement argues against blanket transfer, because the substrate-recognition elements that define each family differ. Nothing retrieved names a substrate, reaction, or regulatory mode for any of these families or any member. No sequence or structure alignment, residue mapping, hit, or quality record was retrieved, so I make no regional, template, or structure-ranking claim.

Evidence needed before transferring substrate specificity or regulation (external to SCOPe except lineage): (1) same-release lineage for the target and reference, which is available here for the families only, not for any specific target protein; (2) substrate-bound or complex structures of a reference with the same substrate class; (3) biochemical activity and selectivity data for the substrate in question; (4) mutagenesis of substrate-contacting and catalytic residues; (5) sequence and structure alignment of the substrate-binding and activation-loop region, not just the fold; (6) primary literature on regulatory inputs such as phosphorylation sites, binding partners, autoinhibition, or lipid-binding modules. SCOPe supplies only the family-level context here.
